introduction.p: The catalog gave us familiar function families. A model is the next step: we choose one of those families because a situation asks for it.
A mathematical model represents selected features of a situation under stated assumptions. Its units should be consistent, and its predictions should be checked against data.

statement.p: A mathematical model is a function, equation, graph, or table used to represent a real quantity.
A model should be judged by four questions:

p.me: \text{How well does it fit the information we have?}

introduction.p: Calculus will later tell us how models change and how their effects accumulate. Before calculus begins, we should learn the main shapes that models can take.

note.title: Modeling lesson
note.p: A formula can be algebraically correct and still be physically wrong outside the range where its assumptions make sense.

exercise.title: What four questions should a model survive?

statement.p: A model represents a situation under stated assumptions. What four checks should be made, and why can an algebraically correct formula give an incorrect physical prediction outside its assumed range?

hint.p: Check assumptions, units, agreement with data, and the applicable range. Algebraic consistency alone does not establish agreement with the modeled situation.

paragraphs.title: A warning
paragraphs.p: Exponential growth can be a good short-term model and a terrible long-term model.

A bacterial population cannot grow forever in a closed dish. A rumor cannot spread to more people than exist. A bank account cannot earn the same interest rate through every possible economic condition.
A model may be useful because it is locally accurate, even when it is not globally permanent. Calculus will often help us decide what “locally” means.

exercise.title: How do you tell linear growth from exponential growth in data?

statement.p: A linear model adds the same amount in equal time steps. An exponential model multiplies by the same factor. In your own words, what should you look for in a table of values, and why can exponential growth be a good short-term model and a terrible long-term one?

hint.p: Constant differences suggest an additive model, whereas constant ratios suggest a multiplicative model. Resource limits or changing rates may invalidate an exponential model beyond the observed data.

subsection.title: Periodic motion
subsection.p: Some quantities repeat.
A Ferris wheel turns. A tide rises and falls. A weight on a spring moves up and down. A point on a rotating tire returns to its starting height again and again.
The basic models for repeating motion use sine and cosine.

paragraphs.title: Residuals: the errors a model leaves behind
paragraphs.p: At input x_i, the prediction error is
These errors are called residuals. A good model should leave small residuals without using a formula that is more complicated than the situation deserves.

p.me: \text{Can I find a formula through the data?}
\text{Does the formula behave reasonably outside the data?}

example.title: a model that fits too well
example.p: Given five data points, it is often possible to find a polynomial of degree 4 that passes exactly through all of them. That does not mean the polynomial is the best model.
A high-degree polynomial may wiggle wildly between data points or make absurd predictions just outside the measured interval. Exact fit is not the same as understanding.
For calculus, the simplest useful model is often better than a complicated perfect fit.

Models give us functions to study. Technology gives us quick graphs of those functions. But a graph on a screen is not the function itself. It is a picture made with choices: a window, a scale, and a finite number of sampled points.
Those choices can hide the truth.

exercise.title: Why is an exact fit not the same as understanding?

statement.p: Residuals are the errors a model leaves behind, and a high-degree polynomial can pass through every data point. In your own words, why should we ask whether a formula explains a pattern rather than only whether it hits the measured points, and what can go wrong just outside the data?

hint.p: Exact interpolation can wiggle wildly between points or make absurd predictions nearby. A good model should leave small residuals without being more complicated than the situation deserves.
